A driver written only against those abstractions cannot cause undefined behavior, *provided the abstractions are sound* and every `unsafe` block honours its contract. That proviso is the whole game; lesson 6 shows what happens when it fails.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
md: Inserting a task into a local DSQ is a commitment. Once there, it waits for that CPU even if another CPU goes idle a microsecond later. Schedulers that want work sharing keep tasks in a shared custom DSQ and move them to a local DSQ only when a CPU asks via `ops.dispatch()`.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Bell-LaPadula: no read up, no write down
md: Bell-LaPadula protects secrecy only. Writing up is allowed, so a low-level process may overwrite a TOP SECRET file it cannot read. Nothing in the model protects the integrity of data; that needs a different model, next lesson.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: The trust algorithm: criteria, scores and context
md: A score hides which factor failed. If a control must always hold (a patched OS for admin consoles, phishing-resistant MFA for payroll), make it a criterion, not a weight that other good signals can outvote.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Threat, vulnerability, exploit, payload and risk
md: A vulnerability is not a risk by itself. A severe bug in software you do not run, or on a machine with no network connection, may carry very little risk. A boring weakness on an internet-facing system that attackers already scan for can carry a lot. Lesson 6 turns this into a patching order.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: EternalBlue and WannaCry: a patch, a leak and a worm
md: WannaCry: one wormable bug, a patch two months old, a leaked exploit, and organisations that had not patched or could not patch old systems. The fixes were basic: patch, remove legacy protocols, filter port 445, segment, back up.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
md: The search policy is a better policy than the network that guided it. Training the network to imitate it is **policy improvement by imitation**. No human labels are used, but new information does enter the loop: from look-ahead, and from the game rules that score every finished game.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: What is safe to cache: scoping, context and invalidation
md: Never let the cache cross users for answers that depend on who is asking: balances, orders, permissions, anything personal. A false hit there is not a quality bug; it is a data leak. Scope by user or tenant, or bypass the cache for those requests entirely.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: XML, entities and XXE
md: Turning off DTDs (DOCTYPE declarations) removes the whole feature: no DTD, no entity declarations, so no external entity fetch and no billion laughs. OWASP's first rule is to disable DTDs whenever possible, and to keep XInclude off too, since it loads documents without any DTD. If a format truly needs DTDs, disable external entities and external DTD loading explicitly, and keep the parser library up to date.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Cache-aware scheduling: queue order sets the hit rate
md: Scheduling cannot create reuse; it can only avoid destroying it. The DFS bound (sum of tree edges) is the floor on prefill work, and ordering decides whether a tight cache reaches it.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
md: A CH query must not stop the first time the two searches meet. The meeting node with the best sum may be found later. Each side stops only when its own queue minimum is at least the best sum found so far.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
md: A SIMD register is a small array of lanes. One instruction does the same operation on every lane. Lane count = register width / element width, so 4, 8 or 16 floats for 128, 256 or 512 bits. Vertical (lane-wise) work is cheap; horizontal (across-lane) work costs shuffles.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Shipping SIMD: -march levels, runtime dispatch, portability
md: Compile for what you can require, dispatch for what you cannot. -march levels give the compiler AVX2 or AVX-512 everywhere but crash on older CPUs; target_clones, __builtin_cpu_supports or is_x86_feature_detected! pick the best version per machine at run time.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
md: Colocation saves GPUs and keeps every GPU busy in a synchronous loop, but it forces phases to take turns and requires offloading. Separate pools only win if you also overlap rollout with training; on their own they just double the GPU count.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: The four triage questions, and the decision flow they make
md: "Expected" needs evidence: a ticket, a calendar entry, a confirmation through a channel the attacker does not control. "The user is an admin, admins do this" is a guess. Attackers who steal admin accounts do exactly what admins do.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Ransomware precursors, and deciding fast: Colonial Pipeline
md: Do not "watch it to learn more" once you see encryption or recovery tampering. Every minute of observation costs files. Escalate immediately with what you know, isolate if your playbook allows it, and let incident response decide about wider containment.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Enforcing sparsity: L1, TopK and JumpReLU
md: TopK fixes L0 = k on every token, even when a token needs more or fewer features. JumpReLU and L1 SAEs let L0 vary, so their reported L0 is an average over tokens.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: The semivariogram: measuring how similarity decays with distance
md: An empirical variogram from a handful of points is very noisy, and the fitted range and nugget can swing a lot with the bin edges or the fitting weights. Look at the plot, try a second binning and treat the parameters as uncertain, not as measured truths.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Draft, verify, keep: the loop with greedy decoding
md: A common bug: after a rejection, keeping the target's distributions for later positions. Those were computed with the rejected guess in the context, so they condition on a token that is no longer in the output. Only the distribution at the first rejected position is valid.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Whisper: a transformer over 30-second spectrogram windows
md: Whisper is an audio-conditioned language model. The encoder turns 30 s of log-mel into 1500 vectors; the decoder generates the transcript token by token, with language, task and timestamps expressed as tokens in the same sequence.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The heap: free lists, chunk headers and where malloc gets memory
md: Stack: LIFO, bounded, freed by returning, one instruction. Heap: any order, any size, any lifetime, paid for with headers, rounding, free-list searches and fragmentation.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Directional ablation: erasing refusal from the residual stream
md: This is dual use. Removing a single direction strips the safety behavior from an open-weights chat model with minimal effect on other capabilities, which the authors read as evidence that current safety fine-tuning is brittle. They also show that adversarial suffixes (strings of tokens, found by automated search, appended to a harmful request to make the model comply) work partly by suppressing this same direction.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Online filtering: EMA as a low-pass, Welford for anomaly flags
md: Online operators keep O(1) state per key and update per reading. Mean and variance via Welford are order-independent; the EMA is not. Both are cheap enough to run per sensor in the stream processor.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Positional encoding, residuals and the full Transformer
md: "Attention is all you need" does not mean attention is all there is. Without the FFN, residual connections, normalization and positional encodings, a stack of attention layers loses most of its parameters, its sense of order, and its trainability.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: BM25's IDF and a full worked example
md: BM25 = sum over query terms of IDF x f / (f + k1 x (1 - b + b x |d| / avgdl)). Three statistics per term and document: f, |d|, and n_t; two per collection: N and avgdl.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
md: The training loop is the generic one (forward, cross-entropy, backward, clip, AdamW step), and the GPT-specific knowledge is in the settings: small normal init with scaled residual projections, decoupled weight decay on matrices only, warmup then cosine decay, and big token batches via gradient accumulation.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Many inputs: partial derivatives and the gradient vector
md: Steepest descent is a local statement. $-\nabla f(2, 1) = (-4, -6)$ does not point at the minimum $(0, 0)$, which lies in direction $(-2, -1)$. In an elongated bowl the gradient mostly points across the narrow valley, which is why plain gradient descent (repeatedly stepping against the gradient, lesson 4) zig-zags.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: Pipes: concurrent processes, sort | uniq -c, and SIGPIPE
md: A pipeline is several processes running concurrently and connected by bounded kernel buffers. Fast writers block on a full pipe; writers to a closed pipe get SIGPIPE. Tools like `sort` that need all their input are where a pipeline stops streaming.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Beyond words: contrastive learning and failure modes
md: Embeddings come from an objective, not from the lookup table. Pick the objective so that items you want close (words in the same contexts, two views of one image, a user and the items they clicked) are pushed together and everything else is pushed apart.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Batching: sharing each weight read across many users
md: Decode is memory-bound, so throughput comes from making every weight read serve many tokens. Batch size is capped by KV-cache memory, and continuous batching keeps that batch full as requests come and go.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why memory is slow and how caches hide it
md: Simplified model. Real CPUs have several cache levels, and **hardware prefetchers** detect sequential and strided access (every k-th element, a fixed step apart) and fetch lines before they are asked for, hiding much of the cost of row order (and some of column order). Measured slowdowns vary by machine; the direction does not.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward models: turning human comparisons into a score
md: A reward model is a learned approximation, not ground truth. Stiennon et al. (2020), an OpenAI paper that used RLHF to summarize Reddit posts, found their reward model preferred longer summaries, and it can be confidently wrong on responses unlike its training data. The next lesson shows what happens when RL optimizes hard against such a model.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity
md: tf rewards a term repeated inside the document; idf rewards a term that is rare across the collection. TF-IDF multiplies them, so a match counts most when the term is frequent here and rare elsewhere.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Addresses and pointers: what int *p actually stores
md: A pointer is a variable whose value is an address. `&` takes an address, `*` follows one, and the pointer's type decides how many bytes are read or written at that address.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Who frees this memory? Ownership and drop
md: Ownership is not about the stack versus the heap as such. A `String` header can live on the stack, in a `Vec` (Rust's growable array), or inside a struct field; wherever it lives, that location is the owner, and the heap block is freed when that owner is dropped.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A vector is a list of numbers and an arrow at the same time
md: Adding vectors of different dimensions is undefined in math. NumPy and PyTorch will sometimes *broadcast* (silently repeat) a smaller array to fit, so shape bugs can produce a result instead of an error. Always know the shape of every array you add.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Where it shows up: linear layers, batches and attention scores
md: Shape errors are the most common bug in ML code. Before running a line like `X @ W.T + b`, write the shapes next to it, `(B,n) @ (n,m) + (m,)`, and check that inner sizes match and the bias length equals the output size.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Fighting overfitting: validation, weight decay, early stopping
md: With adaptive optimizers the two forms of the penalty differ. Adding $\lambda\lVert w\rVert^2$ to the loss and decaying weights directly are equivalent for plain SGD (after rescaling by the learning rate) but **not** for Adam, which is why AdamW decouples weight decay from the gradient step (Loshchilov and Hutter).

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Processes and limited direct execution
md: A system call is not just a function call. It looks like one because the C library wraps it, but inside is a trap that changes privilege level, and the kernel, not the caller, decides which code runs.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
md: Conditioning means restricting attention to the outcomes consistent with what you know, then renormalizing so they sum to 1. Almost every formula in this course is that one idea applied carefully.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND
md: 6ND counts useful model FLOPs, not wall-clock. Real hardware sustains only a fraction of its peak, so time and cost depend on utilization. And at long context lengths the attention term that 6N ignores stops being small. Serving a trained model costs about $2N$ FLOPs per generated token (forward pass only), which matters in lesson 5.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Precision, recall, and why accuracy is useless for search
md: P@k does not average well across queries. If a query has only 3 relevant documents, even a perfect system gets P@10 = 0.3. Also note that trec_eval's P@k pads short result lists with nonrelevant documents: retrieving 15 documents with 4 relevant gives P@20 = 4/20 = 0.2.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: From token vectors to one sentence vector: pooling and cosine
md: Pooling a pretrained language model does not give you a good embedding model. BERT was never trained to make cosine meaningful; the training objective in the next lesson is what does that.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
md: Ties are common on small data. This code picks the pair it encountered first, so a different tie-break or a different word order can produce a different merge list. Real trainers fix a deterministic rule; production implementations also update pair counts incrementally instead of recounting everything, as Sennrich et al. note.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: BatchNorm, LayerNorm and dropout: train mode vs eval mode
md: BatchNorm and Dropout behave **differently in train and eval mode**. `model.train()` and `model.eval()` flip that switch for every such layer at once; forgetting either one is among the most common silent bugs in practice.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: The software supply chain: a map with every attack point
md: Every stage is a trust boundary, and attackers pick the stage with the widest fan-out: one poisoned library, build server or CI action reaches thousands of victims at once. Defence means asking, for each arrow, what proves the thing arriving is the thing you expected.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Provenance and SLSA levels: a signed record of how it was built
md: Provenance moves the question from 'do I trust this file?' to 'do I trust this repository, this workflow and this build platform?', which you can check by machine. npm's documentation is explicit that provenance does not guarantee a package has no malicious code; it makes origin verifiable.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Using synthetic data well: filter, diversify, anchor
md: Synthetic data are useful when an outside signal decides what is kept, diversity is designed in, and real data stay in the training mix. Model collapse is what happens when all three are missing.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When mmap wins, when it hurts, and how to steer it
md: Use mmap for read-mostly data that fits in memory and benefits from sharing. When data far exceeds memory, or you need control over when writes reach disk and how I/O errors surface, explicit I/O with your own buffer pool wins.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Merging overlapping roles: union, gaps and double counting
md: Total experience is the length of the union of role intervals, not the sum of their lengths. Sort by start, sweep, extend with max of the ends, and record gaps as you close blocks.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Search against a PRM, revisions, and compute-optimal allocation
md: These results are for one model family (PaLM 2-S*) with specially fine-tuned revision models and PRMs, on MATH. The qualitative lesson (match the method to difficulty; strong search over-optimizes a weak verifier) is the transferable part, not the exact 4x.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans: surprise, momentum and a forget gate for neural memory
md: Titans' memory update = gradient descent with momentum (carry surprise forward) and weight decay (forget), all gated per token. Momentum keeps writing after a surprising event; forgetting keeps a fixed-size memory from overflowing.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: What a threat model is: four questions before the code
md: Threat modeling happens at design time and keeps happening. A threat model is maintained alongside the system and refined as it changes, not written once for an audit.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Design principles II: least privilege, two keys and shared parts
md: Principles pull against each other. Separation of privilege adds steps that strain psychological acceptability; least privilege adds roles that strain economy of mechanism. Saltzer and Schroeder call them warnings, not rules: when you violate one, write down why the trouble is accounted for.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: The SSD tier, zswap, and running tiering in production
md: Symptoms of thrashing: `pgdemote_*` and `pgpromote_success` both climbing fast at the same time. Pages are moving down and back up. Either the hot set is larger than DRAM, or headroom is too small. Migration itself consumes memory bandwidth on both tiers.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: The TLS 1.3 handshake, message by message
md: Two messages carry the security: the **key shares** create a secret no eavesdropper can compute, and **CertificateVerify** ties that secret to the certificate's key. Without the signature, a man in the middle could run one DH exchange with each side.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: From threads to blocks: the Triton programming model
md: CUDA: *scalar program, blocked threads*. Triton: *blocked program, scalar threads*. In Triton you think about which tile each program owns; the compiler thinks about which thread holds which element.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Everything is a token: Chameleon and Emu3
md: Misconception: "sharing a vocabulary makes images and text equally easy to model." Image tokens have very different entropy (the average surprise of the next token, $-\sum p \log p$: high when many tokens are about equally likely) from text tokens, and the paper attributes the instability exactly to modalities of different entropy sharing one softmax.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Syscalls become function calls: one address space, one privilege level
md: Unikernel speed comes from **removing the user/kernel crossing**, not from a faster CPU path. Gains are largest for small, syscall-heavy requests and near zero for compute-bound code.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Graph traversal: memory layout, cache misses and prefetching
md: In graph search the expensive part per hop is often the first touch of a random vector, not the arithmetic. Contiguous fixed-size blocks, aligned vectors, prefetching and smaller (compressed) vectors all attack that same miss.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: One GRPO step through RayPPOTrainer, call by call
md: Read the source, not just the prose. The reward-function doc says the GSM8K scorer (GSM8K, Grade School Math 8K, is OpenAI's set of about 8,500 grade-school math word problems with numeric answers) gives 0.1 for a well-formatted wrong answer, but in the current `gsm8k.py` the default `format_score` is 0.0. A silent difference like that changes what the policy is rewarded for.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: World models, and why Genie learns one from unlabelled video
md: A learned world model is not the real environment. Ha and Schmidhuber found their agent discovered an *adversarial policy* that exploited flaws in M, doing well in the dream but not in reality. They raised a sampling temperature, a knob that scales how random M's samples are (higher means more random), to make the dream noisier and harder to exploit. Every world model in this course shares this risk.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: A new head and a higher resolution
md: Preprocessing must match the checkpoint. `google/vit-base-patch16-224-in21k` normalizes with mean 0.5 and std 0.5 per channel, while many timm ImageNet models use mean (0.485, 0.456, 0.406). Load the checkpoint's own settings (`AutoImageProcessor` in Transformers, `resolve_data_config` in timm) instead of copying numbers from another model.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Running action chunks in the control loop
md: Temporal ensembling is not a universal upgrade. The pi0 authors tried it early and found it hurt performance, so pi0 executes chunks open-loop: 16 actions then replan on 20 Hz robots (every 0.8 s), 25 actions on 50 Hz robots (every 0.5 s).

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: How vLLM chooses a backend: priority lists and validation
md: Older guides set the `VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND` environment variable. It existed in `vllm/envs.py` up to the v0.14 release and is gone from main. Use `--attention-backend` or `--attention-config` (`-ac`). `AttentionConfig.backend_per_kind` can also set a backend per KV cache group kind, for example a different one for sliding-window MLA layers.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Small text needs pixels: AnyRes tiling and dynamic resolution
md: Tiling only helps up to the largest grid the model was trained with. Beyond that the image is downscaled again, and text that was 10 px tall becomes 5 px tall. Check the preprocessing config of the model you deploy, not just the paper.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Consensus numbers: which primitives can build wait-free objects
md: Compare&swap is **universal**: an object with consensus number at least $n$ can implement any object wait-free for $n$ processes (next lesson). Fetch&add, swap and test&set are not, so Herlihy proves you cannot build a wait-free compare&swap out of them plus registers for three or more processes.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Rolling a 6-hour step out to 10 days
md: Blurry long-range output from an MSE-trained model is not a bug in the network. It is exactly what MSE asks for under uncertainty. Lesson 5 shows how ensembles and CRPS avoid it.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Cookies, sessions, and how Firesheep hijacked them in 2010
md: A session cookie is a **bearer token**: whoever bears (holds) it is, as far as the server is concerned, the logged-in user. No password is needed to use it. Protecting the session ID matters as much as protecting the password, for as long as the session is valid.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: The map: what happens when you open one file on Windows
md: Practise only on machines you own or are allowed to test, ideally a Windows virtual machine you created. The legal line from security-basics applies to every command and tool in this course.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Why wireless is different: a medium anyone in range can hear
md: Wireless security starts from one assumption: an attacker in radio range receives every frame, and can transmit frames of their own. Only cryptography (encryption plus authentication of every frame and of the network itself) changes what they can do with that position.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: iOS: code signing, sandbox, Secure Enclave and BlastDoor
md: iOS security is layered: signed code only, every app sandboxed, entitlements signed in, memory mitigations, keys in a separate Secure Enclave, files encrypted per class, and the riskiest parsers isolated in BlastDoor. Real attacks (lesson 17) need a chain of bugs to get through several layers.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: The Chase-Lev deque: two counters and one CAS
md: Owner and thieves only ever race for the last task. Every other take is a store, a fence and a load with no CAS, and a push needs no read-modify-write at all.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: Where the copies go in a read and write loop
md: Zero-copy does not mean faster for every request. It removes per-byte work but adds per-call and per-page bookkeeping. For small messages the copy is cheap and the bookkeeping can cost more, as lesson 5 measures.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: NLI entailment: is the label a true statement about the text?
md: A multi_label score near 0.6 is not a 60% chance the label applies. It is the entailment share after throwing away the neutral mass, from a model trained on MNLI sentence pairs, not on your labels. Treat it as a ranking score and set thresholds on labeled data.
